sec.title: Background
sec.p: Cytotoxic T-cell-mediated tumor lysis is a key mechanism of oncolytic virotherapy. While oncolytic viruses expressing bispecific T-cell engagers (BiTE) enhance tumor targeting, they lack costimulatory signals, leading to T-cell exhaustion. We developed an oncolytic adenovirus expressing a trispecific T-cell engager (TriTE) to improve antitumor responses in colorectal carcinoma models.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: An oncolytic adenovirus (Ad5-TriTE) was engineered to express a TriTE molecule targeting EpCAM (tumor antigen), CD3ε (T-cell activation), and 4-1BB (co-stimulation). For comparison, a BiTE-expressing virus (Ad5-BiTE) lacking 4-1BB was used. BiTE (αCD3ε-αEpCAM) facilitates T-cell redirection, whereas TriTE (αCD3ε-α4-1BBL-αEpCAM) adds co-stimulation for enhanced T-cell activation. Antitumor efficacy was evaluated in syngeneic and humanized colorectal carcinoma mouse models.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Ad5-TriTE demonstrated efficient tumor infection and TriTE secretion, leading to superior tumor control compared to Ad5-BiTE. Enhanced CD8 + T-cell infiltration and activation correlated with improved antitumor effects in both subcutaneous and peritoneal metastasis models. The humanized version, Ad5-hTriTE, exhibited potent activity in a humanized colon cancer model.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Oncolytic adenovirus armed with TriTE enhances antitumor immunity by integrating costimulatory signaling. Incorporating costimulatory molecules into oncolytic virotherapy may offer more effective cancer immunotherapy strategies.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Oncolytic virus (OV)-based immunotherapy is a novel anticancer treatment that utilizes low-pathogenic viruses to replicate selectively within tumor cells [1]. OVs induce antitumor responses via multiple mechanisms, such as direct tumor cell lysis, indirect immunogenic cell death, and activation of innate and adaptive immune [2]. Currently, several OVs are actively being investigated and tested in preclinical models and clinical trials, such as adenoviruses, herpes simplex virus, and vaccinia virus [1]. Adenovirus, among all of the above, has been one of the best characterized and most promising OV backbones for cancer immunotherapy due to several advantages, including high infectivity, low pathogenicity, and genetic stability [3].

Different classes of oncolytic viruses are currently being examined in solid tumors, including “arming” oncolytic viruses with therapeutic genes. Cretostimogene grenadenorepvec is an investigational adenovirus-based immunotherapy that selectively replicates in cancer cells with retinoblastoma pathway alterations and simultaneously produces granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) [4]. It is tested in combination with pembrolizumab in phase II clinical trials in bacillus Calmette-Guérin unresponsive non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer with carcinoma in situ patients. Patients reported a complete response rate of 57.1% at 12 months and no disease progression or grade 4 side effects in any patients [4]. Now, a number of oncolytic adenoviruses have been approved for clinical use, such as SynOV1.1 and Oncorine [5, 6]. They are mainly used in patients with solid tumors who have failed to respond to conventional radiotherapy or radiotherapy plus chemotherapy in late-stage disease.

Recently, a phase I/II study was conducted to evaluate the safety and feasibility of LOAd703, which is an oncolytic adenovirus encoding CD40L and 4-1BBL for advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. The results showed that among patients treated with LOAd703, not only were no treatment-related serious adverse reactions reported but also more than 90% of patients had an increased proportion of CD8 + effector memory cells and adenovirus-specific T cells, and there was more than a 40% objective response rate [7]. Another phase II study showed that ONCOS-102, an oncolytic adenovirus expressing GM-CSF, plus cisplatin/carboplatin appeared to have greater median overall survival (20.3 months vs 13.5 months) than chemotherapy alone. And increased T-cell infiltration and immune-related gene expression were observed [8]. Hence, engineering OAVs to equip them with immune activators through genetic modification to stimulate CD8 + T-cell activation and reshape the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) is a promising strategy.

Epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM) is an essential transmembrane glycoprotein that is commonly overexpressed in colorectal carcinoma, playing a significant role in tumor progression and immune evasion [9]. Catumaxomab, a trifunctional antibody targeting CD3 and EpCAM, was initially developed for the treatment of malignant ascites but was later voluntarily withdrawn from the market for commercial reasons [10]. CD3 signaling, especially when combined with 4-1BB co-stimulation, robustly activates cytotoxic T cells, enhancing their antitumor capabilities [11, 12]. Additionally, 4-1BB co-stimulation has been shown to activate natural killer (NK) cells, further amplifying their antitumor effects [13]. Solitumab, a bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE) targeting CD3ε and EpCAM, has demonstrated significant tumor volume reduction while increasing cytotoxic T-cell infiltration and activity within the TME [14]. These findings suggest that developing a trispecific antibody that binds EpCAM, CD3, and 4-1BB could maximize cytotoxic T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity in malignancies with high EpCAM expression, such as colorectal carcinoma.

Here, we report the development of an engineered oncolytic adenovirus, Ad5-TriTE, encoding a TriTE (αCD3ε-α4-1BBL-αEpCAM) to drive potent antitumor responses. Our study demonstrates that Ad5-TriTE significantly enhances T-cell infiltration, activation, and tumor regression in aggressive preclinical colorectal carcinoma models.

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: The murine CRC cell line C26 (Fenghui Biotech) was cultured in RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco). Similarly, the murine colorectal carcinoma cell lines CT26 (ATCC) and MC38 (Kerafast), as well as the human CRC cell line HCT116 (ATCC), were maintained under identical conditions. All cell lines were routinely cultured at low passage numbers (< 20 passages after thawing) and confirmed to be Mycoplasma-free before use (Sigma-MP0030).

sec.title: Recombinant adenovirus construction, purification, and expansion
sec.p: The gene constructs encoding the BiTE (αCD3ε-αEpCAM) and TriTE (αCD3ε-α4-1BBL-αEpCAM) antibodies were synthesized by GeneScript (Nanjing, China) and sub-cloned into the pAd5-Ctrl vector to generate the recombinant pAd5-BiTE and pAd5-TriTE shuttle vectors. Viral genomes were constructed by performing long-range (LR) recombination and linearization with Pac I (New England Biolabs) of the pAd/PL-DEST™ backbone vector (V49420, Invitrogen, USA), after which one of the shuttle vectors (pAd5-Ctrl, pAd5-BiTE, or pAd5-TriTE) was inserted into the backbone.

After LR recombination, viral genomes were linearized with PacI (New England Biolabs) and transfected into HEK293 cells until a 90% cytopathic effect was observed for virus rescue. Viral particles were subsequently isolated by iodixanol gradient ultracentrifugation (R714JV, Shanghai Basal Media Technologies Co., China, SW41 rotor, 35,000 rpm, 2 h, 10 °C). Viral titers were determined through a serial dilution assay in 96-well plates containing HEK293 cells (10,000 cells/well). After a 5-day culture period, fluorescence intensity was assessed by microscopy, and titers were calculated using the formula as follows: TCID50 = 102 + (S/N-0.5)/ml, with pfu/ml = TCID50/ml × 0.7, where S is the number of fluorescence-positive wells and N is the number of replicates.

sec.title: Western blot analysis
sec.p: All CRC cell lines were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 1 × 106 cells/well and infected with the recombinant adenovirus (multiplicity of infection (MOI) = 100) for 72 h as previously described. Cell culture supernatants and cell pellets were harvested. Cells were lysed with RIPA buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentrations were determined using the BCA assay. Equal amounts of protein samples were loaded onto a 10% SDS-PAGE gel, separated, and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (Merck Millipore). The PVDF membranes were blocked with 5% skimmed milk (1 h, RT) and probed with the corresponding antibodies overnight at 4 °C. After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:5000, 1 h, RT). Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) was probed as a loading control to confirm equal protein loading. Antibody information is listed in Additional file 1: Table S2.

sec.title: ATP and HMGB1 ELISA
sec.p: CRC cell lines were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 1 × 106 cells/well and infected with recombinant adenoviruses (MOI = 0, 10, 100) for 72 h. Cell culture supernatants were then collected and centrifuged at 300 × g for 5 min to remove debris. Extracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and high mobility group protein B1 (HMGB1) concentrations were measured using an ATP assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) and a mouse acetyl-HMGB1 ELISA kit (cat. no. JL51819-96 T, Jonln, China) according to the manufacturers’ instructions. All experiments were performed in triplicate.

sec.title: IncuCyte analysis of viral copy
sec.p: CRC cell lines were seeded into 12-well plates at a density of 1 × 105 cells/well and infected with recombinant adenovirus at an MOI of 100. GFP fluorescence intensity, representing viral replication, was monitored over 72 h using the IncuCyte ZOOM system (Essen Bioscience), with images captured and analyzed every 8 h.

sec.title: Cell viability assays
sec.p: CRC cell lines were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 104 cells/well and allowed to adhere overnight. Cells were then infected with Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, or Ad5-TriTE at the indicated MOIs for 72 h. After infection, 100 µL of CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay reagent (Promega, G7573) diluted in Opti-MEM was added to each well and incubated at 37 °C for 45 min. Luminescence was measured using a plate reader (560-nm emission, 590-nm excitation) to assess cell viability. Data were normalized to untreated controls. Each condition was tested in triplicate wells.

sec.title: Cytotoxicity (LDH) assay
sec.p: Co-culture experiments were established by mixing tumor cells and lymphocytes at the indicated effector-target (E:T) ratios from 1:1 to 40:1 in complete RPMI-1640 medium. TriTE, secreted from the oncolytic virus, was present in the culture, providing direct activation of CD8⁺ T cells. After 24 h of co-culture, the cell culture supernatants were collected and centrifuged at 300 × g for 5 min to remove debris. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release was quantified using a commercial LDH cytotoxicity assay kit (Beyotime, no. C0016) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. All LDH measurements were performed in technical triplicates and repeated in at least three independent biological experiments.

sec.title: Cell proliferation assay
sec.p: CRC cell lines were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 1 × 106 cells/well and cultured with recombinant adenovirus under the specified conditions. At designated time points, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS and stained with 0.1% crystal violet. After rinsing, qualitative differences in cell proliferation were visually assessed.

sec.title: Mouse models
sec.p: Six- to eight-week-old male C57BL/6 and BALB/c mice were obtained from Nanjing GemPharmatech Co. (Nanjing, China) and housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with controlled temperature (22 ± 2 °C), humidity (60 ± 10%), and a 12-h light/dark cycle. All procedures followed the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee (ACUC) of Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine and Renji Hospital.

Mice were randomized into experimental groups (n = 5–8 per group), and investigators were blinded to treatment assignments. For tumor implantation, 1 × 106 MC38EpCAM or CT26EpCAM-luc cells in 100 μl saline were injected subcutaneously or intraperitoneally (i.p.) into male C57BL/6 or BALB/c mice, respectively. Mice received 5 × 108 pfu of the corresponding recombinant adenovirus via direct tumor injection or i.p. administration on days 7, 9, 11, and 13 post-inoculation. Tumor volumes were measured every 2 days with calipers. All mice were sacrificed after being anesthetized with CO2.

To assess immune cell contributions, 200 μg of anti-NK mAb (A2114, Selleck, USA) or anti-CD8α mAb (A2102, Selleck, USA) was administered i.p. three times weekly for NK or CD8 + T-cell depletion. Depletion was confirmed by flow cytometry analysis of peripheral blood cells, as previously described [15].

A humanized murine model was established in NOD/ShiltJGpt-Prkdcem26Cd52Il2rgem26Cd22/Gpt (NCG) mice (Gempharmatech, Nanjing) by intravenous infusion of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) (Milestone Biotechnologies, Shanghai). Humanized mice were subcutaneously inoculated with 5 × 106 HCT116 cells, followed by intra-tumoral administration of Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, or Ad5-TriTE on days 15, 17, and 19 post-injection. Tumor volumes, body weights, and survival were monitored, with tumor size calculated as length × (width)2/2. Mice were euthanized when tumor volumes reached 2 cm3 or when they became moribund.

Metastatic tumor burden was assessed using bioluminescence imaging with the IVIS 100 system (Xenogen/Perkin Elmer) following i.p. injection of D-luciferin (15 mg/ml, 200 ml per mouse) and was anesthetized with isoflurane. Imaging was performed 5 min post-injection under isoflurane anesthesia, and signal intensities were quantified using Aniview software.

sec.title: Flow cytometry analysis
sec.p: Peripheral blood cells and tumors were collected from sacrificed animals at designated time points. Tumors were dissociated into a single-cell suspension using mechanical disruption followed by incubation with collagenase IV (1 mg/ml) and DNase I (100 μg/ml) in RPMI medium (Gibco) at 37 °C for 1 h, as previously described [16]. Eythrocytes were removed using red blood cell lysis buffer, and the remaining cells were counted, blocked with purified anti-murine CD16/CD32 (BD Biosciences), and stained with the specific antibodies (Additional file1: Table S1). Flow cytometry data were acquired using a FACSCalibur flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) and analyzed with FlowJo v7.6.5. The flow cytometry panel and gating strategy are shown in Additional file1: Fig. S6.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
sec.p: Human CRC tissues were obtained from the Department of Pathology, Renji Hospital, with approval from the Research Ethics Board of Renji Hospital and Shanghai Jiaotong University. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Murine and human tissues were fixed in 4% PFA (no. G1101, Servicebio) and embedded in paraffin blocks. IHC was performed as previously described [17]. Briefly, 5-µm-thick sections were cut from paraffin-embedded blocks, deparaffinized in xylene (10 min, twice), rehydrated through graded ethanol (100% for 3 min, twice; 95%, 70%, and 50% for 3 min each), and treated with 3% hydrogen peroxide to block endogenous peroxidase activity. Tissue sections were then stained for EpCAM, CD45, CD8α, Ki67, and CD69, with antibody details provided in Additional file 1: Table S2.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using the GraphPad Prism 8.2.1 (GraphPad Software, CA, USA). Normality was assessed by the Shapiro–Wilk test. For comparisons between two groups, an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used. For multiple-group comparisons, one-way or two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test was applied. Kaplan–Meier curves were used to assess survival, with statistical significance determined by the log-rank test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM), as specified in the figure legends.

sec.title: Generation and characterization of recombinant oncolytic ADVs
sec.p:
Using homologous recombination, we generated the recombinant oncolytic viruses Ad5-BiTE, expressing CD3ε-EpCAM, and Ad5-TriTE, expressing CD3ε−4−1BB-EpCAM (Fig. 1A). Western blot analysis confirmed the efficient expression and secretion of the recombinant BiTE and TriTE constructs in CT26, MC38, and C26 cells following Ad5 infection. Both constructs were engineered with a His-tag, and specific bands corresponding to the expected molecular weights of BiTE and TriTE were detected, verifying their successful production. (Fig. 1B and Additional file1: Fig. S1A).Fig. 1
Generation of a novel recombinant adenovirus Ad5-αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM and evaluation of its replication and oncolytic capability in colon cancer cells. A Scheme showing the construction of the recombinant type 5 adenovirus expressing a tri-specific antibody containing the EpCaM, 4-1BB, and CD3ε. B CT26 and MC38 cells were infected with the recombinant oncolytic adenovirus at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 20 for 72 h. The supernatant was harvested, after which the expression of αCD3ε-αEpCaM and αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM was detected by Western blotting using an anti-His antibody. And the immunogenic cell death by exposure of calreticulin was detected at 72 h. C The level of ATP in the supernatant of per cell from CT26 cell and MC38 cell after infection for 72 h. D Quantification of supernatant levels of HMGB1 from CT26 cell and MC38 cell after infection for 72 h. E Time course evaluation of total green fluorescent area over 72 h by virus infected on an IncuCyte instrument. Representative images of positive cells at 24, 48, and 72. Variation curves of GFP density under different times. F CT26 and MC38 cells were infected with either Ad5-BiTE or the control virus at a series of MOIs as indicated, and 72 h later, cell viabilities were measured using Cell Titer Glo. Similar results were obtained in three independent experiments. G CT26 and MC38 cells were plated into a 6-well plate and infected with virus at the indicated MOI for 72 h, and oncolytic ability was determined by crystal violet staining

To rule out immunogenic cell death caused by ectopic gene insertions in adenoviruses, we assessed key markers, including calreticulin (CRT) levels, ATP release, and HMGB1 secretion, none of which were significantly induced by the inserted genes (Fig. 1B, C, D and Additional file 1: Fig. S1A and B). We further confirmed that Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, and Ad5-TriTE exhibited comparable replication and oncolytic activity in C26, CT26, and MC38 cells (Fig. 1E, F, Additional file 1: Fig. S1D and E). Minor differences in GFP expression kinetics were observed among the cell lines, which likely reflect intrinsic variability in adenoviral susceptibility. Additionally, crystal violet staining demonstrated MOI-dependent oncolytic activity across all three adenoviruses in these cell lines (Fig. 1G and Additional file 1: Fig. S1C). Collectively, these findings confirm that Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, and Ad5-TriTE share similar replication, secretion efficiency, and oncolytic properties in vitro.

sec.title: Ad5-CD3ε-EpCaM-41BB secretes soluble antibody and increases lymphocyte migration and activationin vitro
sec.p:
To assess the affinity of TriTE for EpCAM, we utilized the CT26 and MC38 cell lines alongside their EpCAM-overexpressing counterparts (CT26EpCAM, MC38EpCAM). EpCAM overexpression in the modified cell lines was confirmed via flow cytometry (Fig. 2A). Purified his-tagged TriTE, produced by HEK293 cells and purified via His-tag, specifically bound to CT26EpCAM and MC38EpCAM (Fig. 2B).Fig. 2
Expression of tri-specific antibody αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM on tumor cells and modulation of immune cell activation. A Construct of EpCaM overexpressing cell lines MC38EpCaM and CT26EpCaM. Cell lines were analyzed by flow cytometry. B Tri-specific antibodies were incubated with EpCaM overexpressing cell line. Flow cytometry is used to determine the binding ability. C Schematic diagram of killing of tumor cells by lymphocytes and antibody co-cultured. D Relative lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) measurements in the co-culture supernatant. Different ratios of effector to target were compared. E LDH was tested in four groups of co-culture system. Bar chats of each group. F Aggregation of lymphocytes observed by Incucyte (MC38EpCAM labeled with CFSE). G, K Flow cytometry analysis for cytotoxicity of CD8 + T cells in the co-culture lymphocytes. Representative images were shown

Spleens were harvested from C57BL/6 and BALB/c mice, and lymphocytes were isolated (Fig. 2C). To determine an optimal effector-to-target (E:T) ratio for further studies, spleen-derived lymphocytes (effectors) were co-cultured with tumor cells (targets) at different ratios, and LDH release was measured at 24 and 48 h. An E-T ratio of 10:1 was found to be suitable, as it led to sufficient LDH release while maintaining cell viability for subsequent analyses (Fig. 2D and Additional file 1: Fig. S2A). Co-culturing Ad5-TriTE, lymphocytes, and CRC cell lines (CT26, MC38, CT26EpCAM and MC38EpCAM) revealed that antibodies secreted by Ad5-TriTE effectively activated lymphocytes in EpCAM-overexpressing cell lines, as evidenced by LDH release assays (Fig. 2E and Additional file 1: Fig. S2B). We also performed crystal violet staining following the co-incubation. In the MC38EpCAM group, Ad5-TriTE exhibited the strongest cytotoxic effect, which was consistent with the LDH assay results (Additional file 1: Fig. S2C). Live cell imaging showed lymphocyte aggregation around CFSE-labeled MC38EpCAM cells, with arrows indicating that BiTE and TriTE facilitated lymphocyte accumulation (Fig. 2F). CFSE labeling enabled visualization of both virus-infected and control MC38 cells under identical imaging conditions for consistent comparison. Flow cytometric analysis was performed after 24-h co-culture of splenic lymphocytes and tumor cells treated with PBS, Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, or Ad5-TriTE. Compared with the BiTE and control groups, the TriTE treatment significantly increased the proportions of CD69⁺ (Fig. 2G), IFN-γ⁺ (Fig. 2H), granzyme B⁺ (Fig. 2I), and TNF-α⁺ T cells (Fig. 2J and K), indicating enhanced T-cell activation and cytotoxicity. However, perforin expression showed no significant difference among the groups (Additional file 1: Fig. S2D).

sec.title: Ad5-TriTE demonstrates superior antitumor activity in murine CRC models
sec.p:
To evaluate EpCAM expression in colorectal carcinoma, we analyzed The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) dataset, which revealed a significant increase in EpCAM mRNA levels in CRC tissues compared with normal colorectal tissues (Fig. 3A). To further confirm this finding, IHC staining was performed on clinical CRC samples and adjacent normal tissues, confirming elevated EpCAM protein expression in tumor tissues (Fig. 3D and E). Notably, high EpCAM protein levels correlated negatively with CD8 + T-cell infiltration, ESTIMATE immune score, and stroma score (Fig. 3B, C, D). These results suggest that EpCAM overexpression is strongly associated with a poor immune environment. The patients with high EpCAM expression might be more likely to benefit from oncolytic virotherapy.Fig. 3
Ad5-αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM has enhanced antitumor activity in colon cancer subcutaneous models. A Gene expression value of EpCaM between normal tissues and tumor samples of TCGA. B Correlation between EpCaM and CD8 + T cells (CIBERSORT) in tumor microenvironment. C The immune infiltration score, including the immune score and stromal score. The analysis was conducted using the ESTIMATE database. D EpCaM expression level verification in clinical samples by immunohistochemical staining. Scale bar, 100 μm. E Immunohistochemical statistics of EpCaM in human patient samples. F The mice treatment scheme. The colon cancer subcutaneous model was established by implantation of 1 × 10^6 cells MC38EpCaM or CT26EpCaM on the right flank of C57BL/6 J and BALB/c mice. When the tumor volume reached over 100 mm3, the tumor-bearing mice were treated with PBS, 5 × 10^8 PFU of Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, or Ad5-TriTE at a 2-day interval for three times via intra-tumoral (I.T.) injection. G Tumor volumes were determined every 2 days. Data are presented as the mean ± SEM. H Kaplan-Meier survival curves of tumor-bearing mice treated with PBS, Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, and Ad5-TriTE. I Body weight changes were determined every 2 days

Next, we evaluate the antitumor efficacy of Ad5-TriTE. We treated CT26EpCAM and MC38EpCAM tumor-bearing mice with PBS, Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, or Ad5-TriTE via intra-tumoral injection every other day for a total of four treatments (Fig. 3F). In the CT26EpCAM model, Ad5-TriTE treatment resulted in significantly smaller tumor sizes and prolonged survival compared to all other groups (Fig. 3G and H). Similarly, in the MC38EpCAM model, Ad5-TriTE treatment also led to significantly smaller tumors compared to PBS and Ad5-Control (Additional file 1: Fig. S3A). While tumors in the Ad5-BiTE group showed a reduction in size, Ad5-TriTE treatment further improved survival outcomes, although the tumor size difference between Ad5-BiTE and Ad5-TriTE was not statistically significant.

Importantly, hexon staining of major organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys, revealed no evidence of organ damage following Ad5-TriTE treatment (Additional file 1: Fig. S3B). Furthermore, neither Ad5-TriTE nor Ad5-BiTE caused significant changes in body weight, indicating minimal systemic toxicity (Fig. 3I).

To further assess the antitumor efficacy of Ad5-TriTE in a metastatic CRC model, we established CRC peritoneal metastases via intraperitoneal injection of CT26EpCAM Luc cells (Additional file 1: Fig. S4A). Bioluminescence imaging on days 4, 9, and 14 revealed a trend toward stronger suppression of peritoneal tumor growth compared to all other groups (Fig. 4A and D). Further analysis of peritoneal metastatic tumors showed that Ad5-TriTE treatment led to a reduction in both the number and weight of metastatic nodules compared to PBS-treated mice, although the differences did not reach statistical significance due to intergroup variability. (Fig. 4B, C, and E). Multicolor immunofluorescence analysis revealed that TriTE treatment was associated with a substantial enhancement of lymphocyte and CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration within peritoneal tumors. Quantitative assessment demonstrated that infiltration levels in the TriTE group were significantly higher than those observed in the PBS and Ad5-Control groups. Compared with the BiTE group, TriTE treatment exhibited a consistent trend toward increased immune cell recruitment. However, this difference did not reach statistical significance, indicating a potential but not definitive advantage of TriTE over BiTE (Fig. 4F, G, H and Additional file 1: Fig. S4B). Collectively, these results demonstrate that Ad5-TriTE exhibits superior antitumor activity in both subcutaneous and metastatic CRC models. It significantly prolongs overall survival, reduces tumor burden, and enhances immune cell infiltration, all while showing no signs of systemic toxicity.Fig. 4
Invivo antitumor treatment of the Ad5-αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM inCT26-EpCaMperitoneal tumor model. A Live imaging of CT26EpCaM peritoneal model with treatment after tumor implantation in days 4, 9, and 14. B Images of metastases from the abdominal cavity of each group mice. C The tumor weight changes during treatment period in each group of mice. D Statistics of average fluorescence intensity of each group in days 4, 9, and 14. E Gross appearance of CT26EpCaM peritoneal tumor model. F Representative image of multicolor immunofluorescent labeling (CD45 and CD8). Scale bar, 200 μm. G and H Statistics of mean fluorescence intensity of CD45 and CD8 in each group. CD8⁺ T cells were scored only when co-localized with CD45 signal and a DAPI-positive nucleus

sec.title: Intra-tumoral injection of ADVs induced the infiltration of immune cells
sec.p:
To investigate the effects of Ad5-TriTE on the TME, we analyzed immune cell infiltration in the CT26EpCAM and MC38EpCAM subcutaneous tumor models (Fig. 5A). Flow cytometry revealed a significant increase in CD45 + immune cells (Fig. 5C and I), CD3 + CD4 + T cells (Fig. 5D, F, J, and K), and CD3 + CD8 + T cells (Fig. 5F and L) following treatment with Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, and Ad5-TriTE. Among these, Ad5-TriTE induced the most robust enhancement of overall immune cell and T-cell infiltration (Fig. 5B and H). Additionally, NK cell infiltration was observed across all three treatment groups. However, there were no significant differences among them in terms of NK cell recruitment. These findings suggest that while all three adenoviral treatments can modulate immune infiltration, the superior antitumor immunity induced by Ad5-TriTE is primarily T-cell dependent rather than NK cell-mediated, underscoring the central role of T cells in driving its therapeutic efficacy.Fig. 5
Ad5-αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM enhanced immune-cell infiltration and activation in the tumor microenvironment. A The treatment scheme. The tumor model was established by subcutaneous inoculation of 1 × 106 MC38 cells into C57BL/6 mice. After 7 days, the mice were treated with PBS, 5 × 108 PFU of Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, or Ad5-TriTE at a 2-day interval three times via intra-tumoral injection. B, C, D, E, F, G Representative images from flow cytometry analysis of tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte. H, I, J, K, L, M, N Flow cytometric analysis of the proportion of the tumor cells, lymphocytes, and their subsets in the tumor microenvironment after the treatment. O Representative multicolor immunofluorescence image showing CD45 (pink), CD8 (red), Ki67 (green), and CD69 (yellow). Scale bar, 200 μm

To further assess the functional activation of tumor-infiltrating T cells, we analyzed the expression of key activation and cytotoxicity markers, including CD107a, IFN-γ, TNF-α, perforin, Ki67, and granzyme B (Fig. 5G, N and Additional file 1: Fig. S5A, B, C, E, F, G). Compared to PBS, Ad5-TriTE treatment significantly increased the percentage of perforin + and granzyme B + CD8 + T cells, suggesting enhanced cytotoxic potential. Additionally, Ad5-TriTE treatment resulted in a higher proportion of TNF-α + CD8 + T cells compared to Ad5-BiTE, further supporting its role in promoting T-cell-mediated tumor killing. These findings indicate that Ad5-TriTE not only drives T-cell proliferation and recruitment into the tumor microenvironment but also enhances their effector functionality.

Interestingly, the expression of CD25, a regulatory T-cell (Treg) marker, in CD4 + T cells was upregulated following Ad5-Control treatment, suggesting a potential increase in immunosuppressive Tregs in the TME (Additional file 1: Fig. S5D). However, in the Ad5-BiTE and Ad5-TriTE groups, the expression of CD25 did not show a significant difference compared to the PBS group. This may be due to the presence of T-cell stimulation signals that partially offset the negative effects of oncolytic virus therapy. A multicolor immunofluorescence analysis revealed that CD45, CD8, Ki67, and CD69 were co-localized in MC38 and CT26 mouse tumor tissues (Fig. 5O and Additional file 1: Fig. S3C). The group treated with the oncolytic virus Ad5-TriTE had a higher proportion of immune cells, CD45 +, and CD8 + T cells compared with the other three controls. At the same time, more Ki67 and CD69 were co-expressed in immune cells, indicating the active proliferation of these cells.

sec.title: The in vivo antitumor activity of Ad5-TriTE depends on CD8 + T cells
sec.p:
To further confirm the crucial role of CD8 + T cells in Ad5-TriTE’s antitumor efficacy, we conducted depletion studies targeting CD8 + T cells and NK cells in the MC38EpCAM tumor model (Fig. 6A). Flow cytometry, performed 4 days after antibody injection, validated successful depletion of CD8 + T cells and NK cells in the peripheral blood (Fig. 6B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I). Interestingly, although the proportion of CD45⁺ cells in the peripheral blood did not differ significantly in the CD8⁺ cell clearance group, the number of CD3⁺ cells was markedly reduced compared with that in the oncolytic virus-treated group (Fig. 6G). Notably, CD8⁺ T-cell depletion completely abolished the antitumor effects of Ad5-TriTE, leading to uncontrolled tumor growth, similar to that observed in untreated mice. In contrast, NK cell depletion had no significant impact on tumor size (Fig. 6J and K). The comparable body weights among groups indicate that CD8⁺ or NK cell depletion did not cause toxicity, and that the observed antitumor effects were not confounded by differences in overall health or treatment tolerance (Fig. 6L). These findings reinforce that while 4-1BB signaling has been reported to enhance both CD8⁺ T cell and NK cell function, the antitumor activity of Ad5-TriTE is primarily mediated by CD8⁺ T cells, with NK cells playing a minimal role in tumor control.Fig. 6
The in vivo antitumor activity ofAd5-αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM depends on CD8 + T cells. A Schematic diagram of the experiment for CD8 + T or NK cell depletion. MC38EpCaM subcutaneous tumor model was established as previously described. Three days post tumor inoculation, mice were injected intraperitoneally (I.P.) with 500 μg of anti-mouse CD8a or anti-mouse NK1.1 mAB per mouse. B, C, D, E The depletion of CD8 + T and NK cells was confirmed by detecting the corresponding cells in peripheral blood by flow cytometry 5 days post the antibody injection. Representative images are shown. F, G, H, I Quantification of CD45 + , CD3 + , CD8 + , and NK1.1 + immune cells in four groups. Each dot represents an individual mouse. J Tumor volumes were determined every 2 days. Data are presented as the mean ± SEM. K Kaplan-Meier survival curves of tumor-bearing mice treated with PBS, Ad5-TriTE, Ad5-TriTE plus anti-CD8α, or Ad5-TriTE plus anti-NK1.1. L Body weight changes were determined every 2 days

sec.title: Adenovirus expressing αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM of human origin attenuates tumor growth in a humanized in vivo colon cancer model
sec.p:
Following our demonstration of the pivotal role of cytotoxic T cells in Ad5-TriTE-mediated antitumor responses in murine CRC models, we next explored its translatability to human CRC cell lines in humanized mice. To achieve this, we engineered replication-competent recombinant adenoviruses expressing human αCD3ε-αEpCAM (Ad5-hBiTE) and αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCAM (Ad5-hTriTE) (Fig. 7A). To determine the baseline EpCAM surface expression, we performed flow cytometry on three commonly used human CRC cell lines, PKO, SW620, and HCT116. Among these, HCT116 demonstrated the highest EpCAM expression, making it the optimal candidate for subsequent experiments (Fig. 7B).Fig. 7
Antitumor effect of Ad5-αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM in a subcutaneous HCT116 humanized mouse colon cancer model. A Scheme showing the construction of a recombinant adenovirus expressing bi-specific antibody αCD3ε-αEpCaM and tri-specific antibody αCD3ε-α4-1BB-αEpCaM of human origin. B Cell surface expression of EpCaM levels by flow cytometry of the human colon cancer cell lines. C Identification of the humanized mouse model of the immune system by flow cytometry. D Schematic diagram of the experiment for the humanized mouse. NOG mice were implanted subcutaneously with 1 × 106 HCT116 cells on day 0. On day 3, 5 × 106 PBMC were injected in vein into mice. On day 9, mice were divided into four groups based on tumor volume and treated with PBS, Ad5-Control, Ad5-BiTE, and Ad5-TriTE (intratumoral). E Tumor volumes were determined every 2 days. Data are presented as the mean ± SEM. F Bar graph of tumor volume in day 13. G Body weight changes were determined every 2 days. H Gross appearance of the HCT116 tumor. I Subcutaneous tumors of mice were identified by live animal imaging. J Representative multicolor immunofluorescence

For in vivo validation, we established humanized NSG mice by tail vein injection of 1 × 106 PBMCs. Seven days post-infusion, flow cytometry of peripheral blood confirmed successful humanization, as indicated by a predominance of human CD45⁺ cells and minimal mouse CD45⁺ cells (Fig. 7C). Humanized NSG mice were then subcutaneously inoculated with 1 × 106 HCT116 cells to generate a tumor model (Fig. 7D). Tumor growth monitoring revealed that Ad5-hTriTE treatment significantly reduced tumor size compared to controls (Fig. 7E and F). Gross tumor measurement and live imaging further confirmed the strong antitumor efficacy of Ad5-hTriTE (Fig. 7H and I). Importantly, no treatment-associated toxicity, including significant body weight loss, was observed (Fig. 7G). Finally, we performed immunofluorescence staining for CD45 + and CD8 + cells in HCT116 tumor tissues to examine the local tumor-infiltrating T cells. We observed that Ad5-hTriTE treatment significantly augmented infiltration of CD45 + and CD8 + T cells into tumors (Fig. 7J). Collectively, these results demonstrate the translatability of Ad5-TriTE as a promising therapeutic strategy for human CRC, reinforcing its potential for clinical application.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: BiTE and TriTE are engineered antibodies designed to simultaneously bind two (bispecific) or three (trispecific) targets, typically involving T-cell receptors (e.g., CD3), a tumor-specific antigen, and potentially a third T-cell or tumor cell surface antigen, to enhance and direct immune-mediated cancer cell killing [18]. Although BiTE have achieved significant clinical efficacy against hematological malignancies, they require continuous infusion due to limited serum half-life, and their efficacy against solid malignancies has been limited, mainly due to physical barriers and a “cold” tumor microenvironment [14]. One strategy to overcome these limitations is to use oncolytic viruses to produce TriTEs directly at the tumor site for more robust antitumor immunity. Oncolytic virus encoding BiTE or TriTE has thus emerged as a promising strategy to enhance immune cell infiltration and stimulate in situ antitumor immunity contained within the tumors [19]. Given the widespread overexpression of EpCAM on multiple solid malignancies, oncolytic viruses encoding BiTE targeting EpCAM-CD3ε were designed and showed encouraging antitumor effects in ovarian and other cancers, including promising results reported by Amgen and others [14]. Similarly, other oncolytic viruses encoding BiTE binding to CD3ε and IL-2 have also reported robust antitumor effects against ovarian cancer ascites by enhancing the cytotoxicity of cytotoxic T, NK, and NKT cells [20].

Additionally, the importance of 4-1BB as a costimulatory antigen on T cells is well established, specifically by promoting T-cell survival via ERK1/2, NF-κB, and Bcl-XL-dependent mechanisms and inducing oxidative phosphorylation-driven metabolism and T-cell-derived antitumor cytokines [21]. Recent studies further revealed that 4-1BB signaling regulates the proliferation and differentiation of exhausted CD8⁺ T cells through canonical NF-κB (RelA and cRel)- and TOX-dependent chromatin remodeling, thereby shaping tumor-infiltrating T-cell dynamics and influencing the response to PD-1 blockade [22]. Building on these insights, we designed a novel Ad5-TriTE, targeting CD3ε, 4-1BB, and EpCAM simultaneously. Our study demonstrates that Ad5-TriTE effectively induces cytotoxic T-cell infiltration and significantly reduces tumor burden in both subcutaneous and peritoneal metastatic CRC preclinical models.

Beyond its efficacy in reducing tumor burden, Ad5-TriTE was shown to substantially alter the TME by increasing the infiltration of CD8 + cytotoxic T cells, a hallmark of effective antitumor immunity. Although we did not observe marked differences in the proportion of cytokine-producing CD8⁺ T cells between Ad5-TriTE and Ad5-BiTE groups, it is important to note that Ad5-TriTE treatment substantially increased the overall frequency of CD8⁺ T cells among CD45⁺ tumor-infiltrating leukocytes. This suggests that the absolute number of IFN-γ⁺ or granzyme B⁺ CD8⁺ T cells was likely higher in the TriTE-treated tumors, thereby contributing to a more pronounced cytotoxic response. Unfortunately, as we did not perform tumor weight measurements or total viable cell counts, we were unable to precisely quantify the absolute number of effector CD8⁺ T cells across treatment groups. Depletion studies confirmed that the therapeutic effect of Ad5-TriTE is predominantly T cell-dependent, as NK cell depletion had no significant impact on tumor size. Importantly, the design of Ad5-TriTE allows for the simultaneous targeting of T-cell activation (via CD3ε), co-stimulation (via 4-1BB), and tumor cell specificity (via EpCAM), highlighting the potential of TriTEs to overcome the immunosuppressive barriers characteristic of solid tumors.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In general, this study underscores the therapeutic potential of Ad5-TriTE, an oncolytic adenovirus targeting EpCaM, CD3e, and the costimulatory molecule 4-1BB. Our findings reveal that Ad5-TriTE significantly bolsters antitumor responses in preclinical models of colon cancer, with evidence of enhanced immune cell infiltration and robust CD8 + T-cell activation. The engineered virus outperformed both the control adenovirus and the bispecific T-cell engager-armed adenovirus, highlighting the synergistic effect of incorporating costimulatory signals in oncolytic virotherapy. Importantly, the humanized version of the virus, Ad5-hTriTE, showed promising antitumor activity in humanized mouse models, indicating a strong potential for clinical application. These results suggest that the integration of costimulatory molecules into oncolytic adenoviruses may represent a strategic advancement in cancer immunotherapy, offering a novel avenue to enhance T-cell responses and achieve more durable antitumor effects.
